q.q: What is the main purpose of the analysis stage?
o: Fully understand the existing system and agree the new system's requirements before design starts
Plan the inputs, outputs, data structures and processes of the proposed new system
Decide whether the proposed system is technically and economically worthwhile to build
Check that the completed system meets the requirements agreed with the client
q.why: Analysis investigates the current system and agrees requirements; feasibility, design and testing are other stages.

q.q: Which is NOT a purpose of analysis?
o: Write the program code for the new system
Identify weaknesses in the current system
Understand the existing system's inputs and outputs
Agree the user requirements with the client
q.why: Coding happens in development, after design.

q.q: Why should the analyst look for the strengths of the current system?
o: To reduce the number of interviews that are needed
Because the client insists that nothing is changed
So good features and efficient practices are kept in the new system
To prove to the client that no new system is needed
q.why: Losing what already works, including efficient unofficial shortcuts, would be a backward step.

q.q: During analysis, the analyst suggests a text-message order-ready alert that the client had not thought of. Which aim of analysis does this meet?
o: Identifying weaknesses
Understanding current inputs
Identifying strengths
Identifying opportunities
q.why: Opportunities are useful new features or improvements the client may not have thought of.

q.q: Why is time spent on a thorough analysis worthwhile?
o: It allows programmers to start writing code before the design is agreed
Misunderstandings found now cost a conversation rather than redesign, recoding and retesting
It means the testing stage can be skipped because requirements are already correct
It guarantees that the client will never change the requirements later on
q.why: Errors in understanding are copied into design, code and tests, so finding them early is cheapest.

q.q: Which document is produced at the end of analysis and signed off by the client?
o: The test log
The system specification
The design specification
The feasibility report
q.why: The system (requirements) specification records the agreed requirements.

q.q: What is a direct data source?
o: Data collected first-hand specifically for the current purpose
Data that the organisation itself has stored in its own records
Data that is bought from a third party organisation
Data that already exists and was collected for another purpose
q.why: Direct data is collected first-hand for this purpose without relying on a third party.

q.q: What is the main benefit of a direct data source?
o: It is always more up to date than any other source
It is free and available immediately
It provides targeted data designed for the purpose
It needs no filtering or analysis at all
q.why: The questions can be designed to collect exactly what is needed.

q.q: What is a typical drawback of an indirect data source?
o: It is very expensive and slow to collect
It may not contain exactly the data needed and must be filtered
It cannot be stored on a computer
It needs questions to be designed first
q.why: It was collected for a different purpose, so it may not fit and usually needs processing.

q.q: A hospital uses patient postcodes from its records to map where an illness is most common. The patient records are…
o: a sink
a primary questionnaire
a direct source
an indirect source
q.why: They were collected to treat patients and are reused for another purpose.

q.q: A café runs a loyalty-card survey to plan its menu. The council later uses the same responses to study sugar consumption. For the council, the responses are…
o: an indirect source, because they were collected for a different purpose
neither, because survey data cannot be reused for a second purpose
a direct source, because the data was collected first-hand by a survey
a direct source, because the council is using it for its own decision
q.why: The test is why the data was originally collected, not who collected it.

q.q: A shop reuses its own till data, recorded to process sales, to decide where to open a new branch. What type of source is the till data?
o: Direct, because it belongs to the shop
Indirect, because a third party collected it
Direct, because it is accurate and up to date
Indirect, because it was collected for processing sales
q.why: An organisation's own records are indirect when reused for a different purpose.

q.q: Why should an analyst brief an interviewee on why they were chosen and how their answers will be used?
o: So that notes do not need to be taken
So that the interview takes less time to plan
To reassure them and encourage honest, open answers
It is a requirement of the Computer Misuse Act
q.why: Some staff fear a new system threatens their job; clarity and reassurance build trust.

q.q: What is a structured interview?
o: An interview held with a group rather than one person
An interview recorded on audio for later analysis
An interview with fixed questions, so answers are easy to compare
A conversation with follow-up questions chosen as it goes
q.why: Structured interviews use fixed questions; unstructured ones are conversations with follow-ups.

q.q: Why do the notes recommend taking notes on a standard response sheet rather than audio recording an interview?
o: Audio recordings are illegal without a court order
Notes are always more accurate than recordings
Audio recording can make people guarded
Response sheets remove the need to paraphrase
q.why: Recording can make people guarded; paraphrasing answers back checks understanding.

q.q: Which questionnaire input type lets a respondent select several options?
o: Slider
Free text
Checkboxes
Radio buttons
q.why: Checkboxes allow multiple selections; radio buttons allow exactly one.

q.q: A questionnaire asks for age early on and date of birth later. Why?
o: To identify each respondent by name
To fill space so the survey looks complete
To check consistency and filter out unreliable responses
Because both are required by data protection law
q.why: Contradictory answers reveal careless or untruthful responses.

q.q: What kind of data do closed questions such as radio buttons and rating scales produce?
o: Qualitative data that is quick to analyse
Quantitative data that needs manual reading
Qualitative data that is slow to process
Quantitative data that is quick to analyse
q.why: Closed questions give quantitative data; open questions give richer qualitative data.

q.q: When is a questionnaire the practical choice of technique?
o: When the analyst needs to probe one expert's knowledge
When users are numerous or spread across several sites
When only three clerks in one office use the system
When the analyst must see how a task is actually done
q.why: A questionnaire puts the same questions to many people.

q.q: What is the Hawthorne effect?
o: Documents being out of date or incomplete when they are sampled
Low response rates to questionnaires that are sent out by email
People changing their behaviour because they know they are being observed
Interviewees saying what they think the analyst wants to hear
q.why: It makes observation potentially unrepresentative.

q.q: How can an analyst reduce the Hawthorne effect?
o: Observe only one member of staff for a single short session
Be unobtrusive, observe several people and observe over a longer period
Tell staff in advance exactly what will be watched and when
Replace observation with audio recording of interviews
q.why: The notes give these three ways of reducing it.

q.q: What is the great value of observation as a fact-finding technique?
o: It shows how work is really done, including shortcuts and workarounds
It reaches many people quickly and at low cost
It shows the volume of data processed each month
It gives anonymous answers that are more honest
q.why: People do not always work the way written procedures say.

q.q: Which technique is best for finding the volume of orders processed each month?
o: Free-text questionnaire
Document sampling
Unstructured interview
Observation for one morning
q.why: Order forms and invoices show volumes directly.

q.q: Observation may be unsuitable when…
o: all work happens in one central office
the analyst has plenty of time available
staff follow written procedures exactly
similar work is done differently at several sites
q.why: Local practices at one site may not represent others.

q.q: Why is document sampling often a sensible first step in fact-finding?
o: It shows how staff really work, including unofficial shortcuts they have developed
It lets the analyst probe the opinions of expert users with follow-up questions
It reaches every member of staff anonymously at very low cost per person
It shows key users, data items, flows, volumes and outputs before other techniques are used
q.why: Documents reveal users, data items, formats, flows, volumes and outputs.

q.q: Which is a weakness of questionnaires?
o: They interrupt staff for hours
They reach only a few people
They cannot be anonymous
Answers cannot be followed up
q.why: Questions are fixed in advance; follow-up is an interview strength.

q.q: Which is a strength of interviews?
o: Thousands of people can easily take part
Follow-up questions can probe interesting answers
Answers are anonymous so may be more honest
Very low cost for each person who takes part
q.why: Flexibility and depth are the main strengths.

q.q: Which technique's main weakness is that the evidence may be incomplete or out of date?
o: Observation of staff at work
Unstructured interview
Online questionnaire
Document sampling
q.why: Records may not reflect current practice.

q.q: Why do analysts usually combine fact-finding techniques?
o: Using more techniques shortens the analysis stage
The law requires all four techniques to be used
Each technique's weaknesses are covered by the others' strengths
Clients will only accept long, detailed reports
q.why: Combining gives a more complete and reliable picture.

q.q: Placed on scales of 'how many people' and 'how much depth', where do interviews and observation sit?
o: Deep but narrow
Broad but shallow
Broad and deep
Neither deep nor broad
q.why: Interviews and observation give depth for few people; questionnaires are broad but shallow.

q.q: Which is a weakness of a questionnaire once it has been sent out?
o: It interrupts each person for a long time
A confusing or leading question cannot be fixed
Respondents can ask the analyst what it means
Its closed answers have to be counted by hand
q.why: Once sent, flaws cannot be corrected and there is no follow-up.

q.q: What is the best technique for finding the breakfast habits of first-year students across all NI universities?
o: Interview each student
Observation
Document sampling
Online questionnaire
q.why: Thousands of widely spread people – only a questionnaire is practical.

q.q: What is the best technique for finding out how staff actually follow the procedure for lifting heavy loads?
o: Document sampling
Observation
Questionnaire
Structured interview
q.why: You need to see what people really do, not what they say they do.

q.q: What does triangulation mean in fact-finding?
o: Interviewing three people at the same time
Using exactly three fact-finding techniques
Drawing DFDs at three levels of detail
Cross-checking a finding from one source against evidence from another
q.why: Triangulation confirms accuracy and consistency.

q.q: A manager says shift swaps are rare, but sampled swap forms show dozens each week. What should the analyst conclude?
o: The contradiction is worth investigating and may point to a problem the new system must solve
The difference does not matter, because shift swaps are outside the system
The documents must be wrong, because managers know their own system best
The manager must be wrong, so further interviews are a waste of time
q.why: Triangulation exposes contradictions, which often reveal the real problem.

q.q: A school wants pupils' honest views on teaching quality. Which technique is most suitable?
o: Observation of lessons
Structured interview with each pupil
Anonymous questionnaire
Document sampling of reports
q.why: Sensitive topics suit an anonymous questionnaire so respondents can be honest.

q.q: A hospital rota follows complex rules that only the rota manager fully understands. Which technique best captures them?
o: Send questionnaires to all nurses
Observe the nurses' shifts
Sample the published rotas only
Interview the rota manager
q.why: Complex expert knowledge is best captured by interviewing the expert.

q.q: Which answer would score full marks for 'Choose and justify a technique' for 1 200 pupils?
o: Observation, because it shows the analyst what really happens in the school
Interviews, because they give the analyst more depth than any other technique
A questionnaire to all pupils, as there are too many to interview and anonymity lets them be honest
A questionnaire, because questionnaires are a very quick fact-finding technique to use
q.why: The answer needs the technique, who it is used with and a justification linked to the scenario.

q.q: What is a stakeholder?
o: Anyone who has paid money towards developing the system
A member of staff who uses the system every day
A shareholder in the company that supplies the system
Any person or group with an interest in a system or affected by it
q.why: Stakeholders include clients, end users, IT staff, customers, suppliers and regulators.

q.q: Which is an external stakeholder?
o: End users
The client's managers
IT support staff
A regulator such as HMRC
q.why: Regulators are outside the organisation.

q.q: Why should end users be involved early in development?
o: They write the system specification themselves
They pay for the system so must approve it
The law requires their signatures on the design
Their needs are captured and they are more likely to accept the system
q.why: Consultation improves requirements and acceptance.

q.q: What is MoSCoW used for?
o: Testing program code
Drawing data flow diagrams
Calculating payback periods
Prioritising requirements
q.why: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time.

q.q: A manager wants strong security with repeated log-ins, while counter staff want to serve customers in seconds. What should the analyst do?
o: Leave the conflict to be resolved by programmers during development
Always meet the staff's needs because they use the system every day
Always meet the manager's needs because managers pay for the system
Record both needs, make the conflict visible and help the client set priorities
q.why: The analyst records each group's requirements, exposes conflicts and helps prioritise.

q.q: What do IT staff typically need from a new system?
o: Management reports and return on investment
Convenience, 24/7 access and privacy
Reliability, documentation and compatible technology
Accurate, timely electronic orders and invoices
q.why: IT staff install, support and maintain the system.

q.q: Which is a non-functional requirement?
o: Respond to a search within 2 seconds
Calculate VAT on each invoice
Allow customers to cancel a booking
Produce a monthly sales report
q.why: Response time is a performance condition.

q.q: Which is a functional requirement?
o: Support 200 simultaneous users
Be available 24/7
Send a confirmation email after payment
Allow only managers to see salaries
q.why: Sending an email is an action the system performs.

q.q: Why should non-functional requirements be measurable?
o: To reduce development cost
Because functional requirements cannot be
To make the specification longer
So that they can be tested
q.why: A measurable requirement can be shown to have been met.

q.q: 'Changes to shared data are visible to all users within two seconds.' Why is this non-functional?
o: It is about sharing data, and all data sharing is non-functional
It sets a standard for an existing function rather than adding a new one
It describes the stored data that the system must hold for users
It describes a new action that the system must carry out for users
q.why: Non-functional requirements describe quality attributes of existing behaviour.

q.q: 'The system must provide a backup facility.' How is this requirement classified?
o: Non-functional, because backup is about security
Non-functional, because it sets a frequency
Functional, because it is something the system does
Neither, because backup is a hardware matter
q.why: Providing a backup facility is an action; adding 'every night' adds a non-functional condition.

q.q: Which non-functional requirement is testable?
o: The website should load fast at busy times
Users should find every page easy to use
The system should be very reliable for users
Pages load within 3 seconds at Monday-morning peak
q.why: Only a requirement with a measure can be checked.

q.q: 'The system must be usable 99.5% of the time.' Which non-functional category is this?
o: Capacity
Performance
Reliability
Availability
q.why: Availability is when the system can be used.

q.q: Which is a functional requirement of a payroll system?
o: Only payroll staff can view salary data
Comply with UK GDPR and tax rules
Complete the monthly pay run within an hour
Calculate net pay from gross pay and deductions
q.why: Calculating is an action; the others are conditions.

q.q: From the ferry company's perspective, which is a functional requirement?
o: Let customers pay by phone wallet
Email customers a confirmation
Let customers choose a cabin
Raise fares automatically as sailings near capacity
q.why: It is something the company wants the system to do; the others are customer-perspective requirements.

q.q: Which stock-control requirement is non-functional?
o: Produce slow-moving stock reports
Record batch arrival dates
Be available during all trading hours
Alert staff at the reorder level
q.why: Availability is a condition, not an action.

q.q: Which is a non-functional requirement for a ferry reservation system?
o: Let customers amend or cancel a booking
Show sailings matching route and date
Never sell the same space twice under heavy load
Email a booking reference to the customer
q.why: This is a reliability condition; the others are actions.

q.q: Which is a functional requirement for a utility billing system?
o: All monthly bills produced overnight
Send a reminder 30 days after an unpaid bill
Card payments processed securely
Calculations must be 100% accurate
q.why: Sending a reminder is an action; the rest are conditions.

q.q: Why would 'a laser printer' not earn a mark as a requirement for a billing system?
o: It should be written as 'an inkjet printer'
Hardware should never be given as a requirement
Printers are a non-functional requirement only
Billing systems do not produce any printed output
q.why: The notes say never give hardware as a requirement.

q.q: Which non-functional requirement for a payroll system is specific enough to earn the mark?
o: It must be secure
It must keep data private
Only payroll staff can view salary details
It must be safe and protected
q.why: 'It must be secure' on its own is too vague.

q.q: At the end of which stage is the system specification produced?
o: Design
Analysis
Feasibility
Testing
q.why: It records the agreed requirements from analysis.

q.q: Which is NOT normally part of the system specification?
o: The finished source code
Constraints such as budget
Context and Level 1 DFDs
Functional requirements
q.why: Code is produced in development.

q.q: How does the system specification help testing?
o: Each testable requirement becomes an acceptance criterion
It removes the need for acceptance testing
It replaces the need for a test plan
It contains the test results for each module
q.why: Each requirement can be checked in the test plan.

q.q: How does the system specification help to control scope?
o: It prevents the client from making any requests
Requests not in it can be identified as changes
It sets the payback period for the project
It lists every line of code to be written
q.why: The specification controls scope by showing what was agreed.

q.q: Which section of a system specification records the budget, deadline, hardware and legislation?
o: Constraints
Schedule
Non-functional requirements
Scope and objectives
q.why: Constraints cover budget, deadline, hardware and legislation.

q.q: Why does the system specification help avoid disputes later?
o: It contains the finished system's source code
It is written after the system is tested
It is signed by end users rather than the client
It records the agreement between client and developer
q.why: It records what was agreed, so both sides can refer to it.

q.q: Traditionally, what happened if a client asked for extra features not in the specification?
o: Penalties or revised charges applied
The project was cancelled automatically
The features were added free of charge
The supplier ignored the request entirely
q.why: The specification was a two-way contract.

q.q: Which change has made specifications less prescriptive?
o: The abolition of software contracts
The move to Agile, iterative development
Faster hardware for running code
A fall in the number of software suppliers
q.why: Agile expects requirements to evolve.

q.q: Why did the traditional, rigid specification suit the past?
o: There were few suppliers, who planned their workforce around fixed deliverables
There were many suppliers, so clients could easily switch between them
Software skills were widespread so changes could be made cheaply
Agile methods made it simple to change requirements during a project
q.why: Few suppliers needed fixed plans and timescales.

q.q: In what way was the traditional specification a two-way contract?
o: The client could not demand extra features, and the supplier had to deliver everything specified
The client wrote the code and the supplier tested it before release
The supplier could add features and the client had to pay for them
Both sides could change requirements at any time without charge
q.why: The agreement bound both sides.

q.q: How is change treated in an Agile-era specification?
o: Forbidden once coding has started
Treated as a breach, with penalties applied
Ignored until the final acceptance test
Expected, and handled by change control and reprioritisation
q.why: Agile-era specifications build in ways to change requirements.

q.q: Which type of project still suits a traditional, fully detailed specification?
o: A competitive app whose features keep changing
A safety-critical system with stable requirements
A website whose users' needs are evolving
A start-up product still finding its market
q.why: Traditional specifications suit stable, well-understood or safety-critical requirements.

q.q: Which is a purpose of a data flow diagram?
o: To show the decisions made in an algorithm
To show the order in which instructions execute
To show how a system interacts with external entities
To calculate the payback period of a project
q.why: DFDs show data exchange with entities outside the boundary.

q.q: Why can clients usually understand DFDs?
o: They show every decision in the system
They are written in program code
They use only a few simple symbols
They are always drawn in colour
q.why: Simplicity makes them good communication tools.

q.q: Which feature belongs on a flowchart but NOT on a DFD?
o: An external entity drawn as an ellipse
A decision with yes/no branches
A data store with an ID such as D1
A data flow labelled with a noun
q.why: DFDs do not show decisions or sequence.

q.q: In which stage are DFDs mainly used, compared with flowcharts?
o: DFDs in design for a single process; flowcharts in analysis for the whole system
DFDs in analysis to model a whole system; flowcharts in design for a single process
DFDs in implementation for training; flowcharts in feasibility for costs
Both are used only in testing to check that the code is correct
q.why: DFDs model systems during analysis; flowcharts plan algorithms in design.

q.q: How do DFDs feed directly into design?
o: Processes become modules and data stores become files or tables
Flows become loops and stores become decisions
Entities become modules and flows become tables
Processes become tables and stores become modules
q.why: The notes state processes become modules and stores become files or tables.

q.q: A carefully drawn DFD of the current system shows a store that is written to but never read. What has the DFD helped reveal?
o: An entity outside the system boundary
Wasted effort in storing unused data
A decision missing from the algorithm
A bottleneck caused by too many inputs
q.why: DFDs reveal duplicated work and data stored but never used.

q.q: An external entity that only receives data from the system is a…
o: data store
process
sink
source
q.why: Sinks receive data; sources supply it.

q.q: Which is a correctly named DFD process?
o: Check stock level
Stock file
Customer order details
Stock level report
q.why: Processes are named with verb phrases.

q.q: Which is a correctly labelled data flow?
o: Order details
D1
Process order
Send
q.why: Flows are labelled with noun phrases naming the data.

q.q: How is a data store identified on a DFD?
o: An ID such as D1 and a name
A verb phrase and a number
A decision symbol
A short diagonal line
q.why: Stores have unique identifiers such as D1, D2.

q.q: In CCEA textbook notation, how is a DFD process drawn?
o: An ellipse with its name
A rectangle with a numbered strip at the top
An arrow labelled with the data
An open-ended rectangle with an ID box
q.why: Ellipses are entities, open-ended rectangles are stores and arrows are flows.

q.q: A customer sends an order and receives an invoice. What is the customer?
o: Both a source and a sink
A data store, as it holds the order
A sink only, as it receives the invoice
A source only, as it sends the order
q.why: Many entities both supply and receive data.

q.q: How many processes appear on a context diagram?
o: Exactly one
One per entity
None
Two to four
q.why: The whole system is shown as a single process.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a context diagram?
o: To show the order of processing
To define the system's boundary and scope
To list the test data to be used
To show every file the system uses
q.why: It shows what is inside and outside the system.

q.q: A fast-food customer pays the attendant and receives a receipt. On the context diagram, 'Receipt' is a…
o: external entity
process
data flow from the system to the Customer
data store
q.why: It is data leaving the system to a sink.

q.q: Why are data stores normally left out of a context diagram?
o: The aim is to show scope, not internal workings
Context diagrams never involve stored data
Data stores can only appear on flowcharts
Stores are always shown as entities instead
q.why: The context diagram shows the boundary.

q.q: On a context diagram, a customer pays a card provider. How should this be shown?
o: As a data store between the two entities
As a second process for payments
As data passing through the system, not directly between entities
As a direct flow from Customer to Card Provider
q.why: Entities never connect directly to each other on a DFD.

q.q: What stays the same when a context diagram is exploded to Level 1?
o: The data stores and their identifiers
The internal flows between the processes
The external entities and external flows
The number and names of the processes
q.why: Entities are outside the system; external flows must balance.

q.q: A context diagram shows 'Invoice' going to Customer, but the Level 1 diagram does not. Which rule is broken?
o: The naming rule for flows
No rule – it is allowed
Balancing
The store read/write rule
q.why: Every external flow must reappear at Level 1.

q.q: How are Level 1 processes usually numbered?
q.why: Level 2 would use 2.1, 2.2… when process 2.0 is exploded.

q.q: What is added when a context diagram is exploded into a Level 1 DFD?
o: Sub-processes, data stores and internal flows
New external entities and new external flows
Only further external entities
Decision symbols and the order of events
q.why: Level 1 adds sub-processes, stores and internal flows but keeps the same entities.

q.q: In the Glens Kayak Hire Level 1 DFD, which process handles the 'Weekly hire report' sent to the Manager?
o: 3.0 Produce report
0 Glens Kayak Hire
2.0 Take payment
1.0 Check availability
q.why: The report flow is connected to process 3.0 Produce report.

q.q: If process 2.0 were exploded into a Level 2 DFD, how would its sub-processes be numbered?
q.why: Level 2 sub-processes of 2.0 are numbered 2.1, 2.2…

q.q: Which flow is valid on a DFD?
o: Customer → D1 Orders
Customer → 1.0 Take order
Customer → Supplier
D1 Stock → D2 Orders
q.why: Every flow must start or end at a process.

q.q: A process with inputs but no outputs is called a…
o: sink
miracle
black hole
data store
q.why: It absorbs data and produces nothing; a process with only outputs is a miracle.

q.q: A data store is written to but never read. What does this suggest?
o: It should be drawn as an entity
The store serves no purpose, so a flow or process is missing
Nothing is wrong with the diagram
The DFD balances correctly
q.why: Every store should be written and read somewhere.

q.q: A DFD shows 'Customer → D1 Orders file', labelled 'Order'. What is the correct fix?
o: Insert a process such as 1.0 Record order between them
Relabel the flow with a verb such as 'Send'
Draw the customer as a data store instead
Reverse the arrow so it goes from the store
q.why: Entities cannot connect directly to stores; data must pass through a process.

q.q: A DFD shows a flow directly from D1 Stock file to D2 Reorders file. What is the correct fix?
o: Merge the two stores into one store
Insert a process such as 3.0 Check reorder levels
Replace D2 with an external entity
Label the flow 'Check reorder levels'
q.why: Store-to-store flows are not allowed; a process must be inserted.

q.q: A process on a DFD is named 'Customer'. What is wrong, and how should it be corrected?
o: Processes must be ellipses, so redraw it as an entity
Processes must be numbered D1, so rename it 'D1 Customer'
Processes must be nouns, so rename it 'Customer details file'
Processes are actions, so rename it with a verb, e.g. 'Register customer'
q.why: Processes are named with verb phrases.

q.q: When interpreting a DFD of the current system, a process with many inflows may suggest…
o: a bottleneck
